response.text:
I'll work through each draft chapter systematically, applying the gate test rigorously and checking only for structural damage, not mere compression.

---

**Ch 004 Draft — checks:**

- The Wolfshiem lunch scene: "He peered about the room as if he might take one short glance beneath our own table." In the source, Wolfshiem's eye-roving is narrated over several paragraphs, and "beneath our own table" is the culmination. In the draft this is collapsed into the introduction paragraph, before the Metropole exchange — but the Metropole exchange is an authorized cut (Wolfshiem's Metropole reminiscence). The sentence still parses and a reader can follow it.

- "but I like across the street better—full of memories." The source has Wolfshiem say "full of memories" as a separate beat after Nick asks "What place is that?" / "The old Metropole." That exchange is cut (authorized). In the draft, the phrase "full of memories" is appended to Wolfshiem's line without any referent for what place is "across the street." A reader has no way to know what place Wolfshiem means — it's never named, the question was cut. However, this is a direct residue of the authorized Metropole digression cut. **Authorized cut residue — not a finding.**

- "Gatsby leaned toward me. 'I'm afraid I made you a little angry this morning in the car.'" — This is after the Wolfshiem lunch intro paragraph but before Nick's complaint. The ordering is compressed but parses.

- "He lifted his cuffs." — In the source, Wolfshiem says "I see you're looking at my cuff buttons" and Nick says he hadn't been. The draft cuts Nick's denial but keeps the line. "He lifted his cuffs" appears to follow from his own mention of cuff buttons; a reader can follow. Not a finding.

- Jordan Baker's narration: "After that winter there were rumours—how her mother had found her one night packing…" The source has "By the next year I had a few beaux myself… She went with a slightly older crowd… Wild rumours were circulating about her." The draft cuts the transition "By the next year… she didn't play around with the soldiers any more" and jumps to "After that winter there were rumours." The antecedent of "that winter" — established as the winter when Daisy was prevented from going to New York — is present in the immediately preceding sentence ("she was prevented and would not speak to her family for weeks"). So "After that winter" refers back to that same winter. A reader can follow this. Not a finding.

- "Gatsby quickly produced a book. 'Look at this. Here's a lot of clippings—about you.'" In the source Gatsby shows a scrapbook. The draft says "produced a book" — a reader can understand this is a scrapbook of clippings from context. Not a finding.

**Ch 005 Draft — checks:**

- "I walked out the back way and ran for a huge black knotted tree. Once more it was pouring. There was nothing to look at except Gatsby's enormous house, so I stared at it, like Kant at his church steeple, for half an hour. Americans, while willing, even eager, to be serfs, have always been obstinate about being peasantry." 

In the source, the "Americans… peasantry" line is the conclusion of a paragraph about a brewer who built the house, tried to get neighbors to thatch their roofs, failed, and "went into immediate decline" — the remark is explicitly the narrator's gloss on *that story*. In the draft, the brewer story is entirely cut. The aphorism "Americans, while willing, even eager, to be serfs, have always been obstinate about being peasantry" appears with no setup — no brewer, no thatching scheme, no founding-a-family ambition. The sentence reads as a complete non-sequitur: Nick stares at the house for half an hour, and then this remark appears with no logical or narrative connection to anything in the draft. There is no "broken pivot" connective, but the issue is more a **missing definitional gloss**: the aphorism is a general observation the source anchored to a specific illustrative anecdote; without that anchor the sentence has no discernible referent in the draft and a reader genuinely cannot understand what thought it concludes or why it appears here.

This is not an authorized cut — the brewer anecdote is not on the authorized removal list.

- "We'll have someone play the piano." In the source it is Klipspringer (authorized removal) by name. The draft anonymizes to "someone." The player is then referred to as "the player" who "turned on the bench." This is slightly odd but a reader can follow that "someone" played the piano and that person is "the player." Not a finding per the gate test — Klipspringer is an authorized removal.

- "In Gatsby's apartment I saw how he revalued everything in his house according to the measure of response it drew from her well-loved eyes." The source attributes this perception to the narrator observing Gatsby. In the draft it is rendered as "I saw how he revalued" — this is a slight restructuring but parses and means the same thing. Not a finding.

- "It's stopped raining." / "Has it?" — These are attributed in context (Gatsby speaks first, then responds to himself when realizing the sunshine). In the draft, the first "It's stopped raining" has no speaker tag. In the source it is Nick who says it. In the draft it appears as a free-floating sentence. A reader may be briefly uncertain who says it, but in context (Nick has just returned, sees the scene changed, and makes an observation) it is attributable to Nick. Borderline, but not genuinely confusing — less ornamented rather than broken.

---

**Valid finding:**
